questions.question: What is the main purpose of a vector commitment?
options: Compress a list losslessly into a smaller list
Commit to an ordered list and later prove a single entry with a short proof
Encrypt a list so only the owner can read it
Generate a random value from a list deterministically
questions.explanation: A VC lets you publish one commitment to a whole vector and later open one index with a succinct proof.

questions.question: In a Merkle-style construction, how big is a single opening proof (roughly) for a vector of length n?
options: O(1) hashes, independent of n
O(log n) hashes along a path to the root
O(n) hashes, one per element
O(n log n) hashes due to rehashing the whole tree
questions.explanation: A Merkle opening is a root-to-leaf path, which has length proportional to log2(n).

questions.question: Which API matches the idea of a vector commitment most closely?
options: commit(v) -> root; open(v, i) -> (value, proof); verify(root, i, value, proof, n) -> bool
hash(v) -> root; decrypt(root) -> v
sign(sk, v) -> sig; verify(pk, sig) -> bool
encrypt(pk, v) -> c; decrypt(sk, c) -> v
questions.explanation: A VC has a commitment plus an opening/verification procedure per index.

questions.question: Why does the lesson's `leaf_hash` include the index `i` when hashing a leaf?
options: To make the commitment hiding
To bind the value to a specific position so proofs cannot be reused for other indices
To speed up hashing by avoiding internal nodes
To allow verifying without knowing the vector length n
questions.explanation: Including `i` provides index binding: a proof for position j should not verify at position i.

questions.question: What does 'length binding' mean in this lesson's commitment root?
options: The proof length is always the same for any n
The commitment is hashed together with n so the same Merkle root cannot be reused under a different vector length
The commitment leaks the length but hides values
The verifier can reconstruct the vector length from the proof alone
questions.explanation: The final root is `H(tag || n || merkle_root)`, so changing n changes the commitment even if the underlying tree hash matches.

questions.question: What is 'domain separation' in this Merkle-based VC?
options: Using different network domains for different nodes
Using different hash functions for each tree level
Prefixing inputs (e.g., 'VC:leaf', 'VC:node', 'VC:root') so different hash contexts cannot be confused
Using base64 instead of hex encoding
questions.explanation: Tags/prefixes ensure leaf hashing, internal-node hashing, and the final root hashing are distinct domains.

questions.question: Attack question: If a design hashes leaves as H(str(i) + value) with no length-prefixing, what is a realistic risk?
options: Ambiguous encodings can let an attacker craft different (i, value) pairs that hash the same input bytes before hashing
It becomes information-theoretically hiding
Merkle proofs become constant size
SHA-256 stops being collision resistant
questions.explanation: Without an unambiguous encoding, different structured inputs can map to the same byte string before hashing, enabling malleability bugs.

questions.question: If you mutate one element of the vector after publishing the commitment, what should happen?
options: The same root remains valid, but proofs change
The same proofs remain valid, but the root changes
Both the root and any old openings for that index should fail to verify under the new root
Nothing changes because commitments are randomized
questions.explanation: A binding commitment changes when the underlying vector changes; old openings should not verify against a different commitment.
